an1.235:1.1: Mahāpajāpati was the Buddha’s foster-mother, sister of his birth mother Māyā. She is honored in the tradition as the first nun, the founder of the bhikkhunī order ([an8.51]()). Though mostly remembered as the Buddha’s mother ([mn142]()), her own verses deconstruct her motherhood, relating how she has previously been a “mother, a son, a father, a brother, and a grandmother” but now has transcended all such states ([thig6.6:3.1]()).
an1.236:1.1: Khemā, whose name means “sanctuary”, was praised for her teaching to King Pasenadi ([sn44.1]()). Her verses are at [thig6.3](); see [sn17.24:1.7]().
an1.237:1.1: Uppalavaṇṇā’s skill in psychic powers kept her fearless when demolishing Māra ([sn5.5]()). Her verses are at [thig11.1](), and she was as a teacher of nuns ([thig13.5:27.3](), [pli-tv-kd20:8.1.1]()). A Vinaya story shows her gratitude to the Buddha ([pli-tv-bu-vb-np5:1.1.1]()). She was a survivor of sexual assault ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pj1:10.5.1]()).
an1.238:1.1: Paṭācārā’s verses recount her experience of awakening ([thig5.10]()). She is honored as a teacher by many students in the Therīgāthā ([thig5.11](), [thig5.12](), [thig6.1](), [thig7.1]()). This supports the idea that she was an expert in the Vinaya. However, she is not mentioned at all in the Vinaya Piṭaka. This suggests that the Vinaya texts that we have today, which were redacted by the monks, can be quite separate from the traditions of the nuns.
